Most of what your AI agent loads, it never uses.

skillreaper finds the unused skills, MCP servers and subagents quietly filling your context window - proven from your own session transcripts - and prunes them reversibly. Hooks and always-loaded prose are listed in the report, not judged or pruned.

Zero config.** It reads your real session transcripts, finds every skill / MCP / agent your AI loads but never fires, and shows you exactly what it costs you. ## What it does skillreaper is a **measuring instrument** for your agent's context window. Pruning is one of the things you do with the measurement, not the point of it. The whole surface, in the order you use it: | Stage | Command | What it answers | |---|---|---| | **Measure** | `reap` | What do I load, what actually fires, what does the dead part cost per session? | | | `reap gap` | What share of each category is ever used, and which MCP tools fire but return noise? | | | `reap by-project` | Which project is actually firing each skill? | | **Decide** | `reap why ` | Why did *this* item get *this* verdict, on what evidence? | | **Act** | `reap prune` | Quarantine the dead items, reversibly | | | `reap mute ` | Strip a heavy rarely-used description, keep the skill callable | | **Engineer** | `reap route` | Propose a lazy-load routing plan for a library too big to prune flat | | | `reap apm` | Emit a proposed APM `apm.yml`, so a team reproduces one lean set | | **Compare** | `reap snapshot` | Keep this run, so a later one has something to be measured against | | | `reap diff` | What appeared, left, changed verdict, and did anything come back after a prune | Everything above the **Act** row is read-only. You can run the entire measurement side without changing a single file.
## What it reads, what it writes | Read-only, changes nothing | Writes, always reversible | |---|---| | `reap` 1 | `reap prune`  ↔  `reap restore --all` | | `reap gap` 1 | `reap mute `  ↔  `reap unmute ` | | `reap by-project` 1 | `reap keep `  ↔  `reap keep --remove ` | | `reap why ` 1 | `reap install-hook`  ↔  `reap uninstall-hook` | | `reap route` 1 | `skillreaper` / `reap menu`: the same writes, chosen on one screen, undone from it with `u` | | `reap apm` 1 | | | `reap manifest ` 1 | | | `reap share` 1 | | | `reap snapshot` 1 | | | `reap diff` | | **Nothing is deleted unless you ask for exactly that.** `reap prune` moves files into a `reaped/` directory with a versioned manifest, `reap mute` keeps a backup of the description it strips, and `reap uninstall-hook` removes only skillreaper's own entry, leaving your other hooks alone. The one exception is the one you have to name: `reap delete `, or `d` in the menu, removes an item for good, says so in red, and asks first. Every edit of an existing file is **atomic** (temp file + rename), so an interrupted prune, mute, or hook edit leaves the original file intact, never a half-written mix, and every write stays **inside your home folder**, in the files of the tools it reads (`~/.claude`, `~/.claude.json`, `~/.codex` and the like). Removing an MCP server edits `~/.claude.json` and keeps a copy of the whole file in `~/.claude/reaped/backups/` until you restore that server; if Claude Code changes the file while reap is editing it, reap writes nothing and asks you to run the command again. One command is not local, and it is not in the table: `reap reinvest`, which is experimental. It asks Claude, through `claude -p`, to read your sessions and write a skill for work none of yours covers, and with `--online` it searches skills.sh. Nothing else here calls a model or the network. (The menu's plugin switch runs `claude plugin disable`, Claude Code's own command for that.) 1 The only files a read-only command writes are skillreaper's own: ~/.claude/reaped/nudge-state.json, which the default report touches so a hint it already showed you does not repeat; a parsed-transcript cache in your user cache folder, which keeps the next run fast; an evidence record in your user config folder, which remembers uses older than your transcripts; and the snapshot reap snapshot exists to write. None of them touches your stack. --no-nudge (or SKILLREAPER_NO_NUDGE=1) turns off the first and --no-cache the second. No command in either column sends anything over the network.
## First 60 seconds Three commands, in this order: measure, decide, act. Only the third one writes anything, and it prints its own undo line. ```bash reap reap why import-timesheet reap prune ``` `import-timesheet` stands for any name in your own report. Or all three on one screen: `skillreaper`, [the menu](#the-menu). With `npx` and nothing installed there is no `reap` on your PATH: write `npx skillreaper` where these lines say `reap` (`npx skillreaper why `). **1. `reap`** prints the report: the same rows as the block at the top of this page (that one is `reap --agent`), grouped by verdict, with the reason in each group's title and in a NOTE column. It shows the whole case for one item, so you are not trusting a label: ``` skill:import-timesheet verdict REAP(unused) reason zero uses in the evidence window token weight ~185 tok (description: 684 chars) sessions 34 total in window uses 0 last seen never installed 2026-07-01 (60 days ago) grace period expired (grace: 14 days) keep-list no claude-md not referenced → safe to prune. run: reap prune ``` **3. `reap prune`** asks before it moves anything, quarantines what you confirm into `reaped/`, and ends by printing `reap restore --all`. ## Why this exists ### Why I built this I was running out of context budget on every session. I had accumulated skills, MCP servers, and agents over months most of them experiments I'd forgotten about or be too busy to change it. Every new session loaded all of them, burning tokens before I'd typed a single message. I needed to know which ones were actually firing and which were just dead weight. Nothing existing told me that from transcript evidence. So I built it. It now supports every platform in the table below, and ships on Homebrew, npm, and as a static binary for every major OS.
### Two costs of context bloat **Wrong-tool picks.** Buried in a wall of irrelevant options, your agent wastes turns reaching for the wrong tool. More turns = slower, costlier, sloppier runs. This isn't about pennies - it's about work quality. **Wasted tokens.** Dead instructions eat context every session and hurt prompt-cache hit rate. A typical setup: - 382 items loaded - 369 never fired (96 %), of which 367 marked REAP - 19 755 tok/session dead - ~1 087 000 tok/month burned on irrelevant instructions - ~$3.26/month, ~$39/year - the same waste priced instead of counted

The money line is one measurement of one stack, n=1, and the weakest number here: 19 755 × 55 × $3.00 ÷ 1e6 - input tokens only, at claude-sonnet-4-6's $3.00/MTok default, with tokens estimated as ceil(chars / 3.7) and the monthly session count extrapolated from a 30-day window. Change the model, the price, or how much you work and it moves; the item and token counts do not. See Limitations.

Measured on my own setup - 55 sessions over 30 days, 2026-08-23. Run reap to see yours.

skillreaper measures both, from evidence - no guessing. > `reap` points at the waste. You decide what goes.
### Privacy **100 % local**, with one exception you start by hand. Zero telemetry, zero uploads. Reads config files and session transcripts on disk, and your data never leaves your machine, except through `reap reinvest`: it is experimental, says so on its first line, and sends Claude, through `claude -p` on your own Claude Code account, excerpts of your sessions (with the keys it recognises removed first) and the names and descriptions of your installed skills. With `--online` it also sends search words drawn from them to skills.sh (and, with `--mcp`, the MCP registry, then asks npm, PyPI and GitHub about the servers it finds), and says that too on its first line. It keeps what it read of your sessions, with the keys removed, in `sessions_memory.json` under reap's state folder (`~/Library/Application Support/skillreaper/reinvest` on macOS), readable by you alone, so that a kind of work is still known after Claude Code deletes the transcripts.

## Beyond pruning ### route - context engineering for large tool libraries After pruning, a library of hundreds of legit skills still grows resident context linearly. `reap route` proposes a category-router organization driven by **real firing evidence**, not text similarity: frequently-fired skills stay exposed; the rare long tail is pushed behind leaf routers (grouped by namespace, else dominant firing project) loaded on demand. It is strictly opt-in and secondary to pruning - and below ~150 skills, native loading is usually enough, so the plan says so. ### snapshot and diff - what changed since last time A report is a photograph. The questions that recur are comparative: did a pruned item come back, is the bloat growing or shrinking after a prune. `reap snapshot` writes the run's `--json` payload beside the evidence digest. `reap diff` compares two of them, newest against previous by default, and reports what appeared, what left, what changed verdict, and the movement in dead tokens and utilization. The case it exists to catch leads the output: **an item that is back after being pruned**. Plugin and marketplace updates reinstall silently, and that line is read from the prune manifest rather than guessed from the two snapshots, so it says "this tool removed it and it returned" rather than "something is different". `reap uninstall-hook` removes only the skillreaper entry - other hooks untouched. ## Transparency and internals ### Platform support | Platform | Full support | |---|---| | **Claude Code** | ✅ | | **Codex CLI** | ✅ for what was used (its history shows what fired, not everything that was used, so an item with no use there surfaces as REVIEW, never REAP or MUTE) | | **Hermes** | Inventory only (session history is in `state.db`, which skillreaper does not parse yet, so its items surface as REVIEW, never REAP) | | **OpenCode** | ✅ (usage evidence needs the `sqlite3` CLI; inventory-only without it) | | **Cursor** | Inventory only (no local transcripts) | | **OpenClaw** | Inventory only (no session history) | | **Gemini CLI** | Inventory only (session history is stored in a layout skillreaper does not parse yet, so its items surface as REVIEW, never REAP) |
### How the evidence is gathered 1. **Auto-detect** - probes every known config directory. Only installed platforms are scanned. No flags needed. 2. **Inventory** - scans skills, agents, MCP servers, hooks, and prose files across all detected platforms. 3. **Evidence** - parses JSONL session transcripts (Claude Code, Codex CLI). Counts `tool_use` blocks and command invocations with timestamps. OpenCode's SQLite history is read via the `sqlite3` CLI (read-only) when it is on `PATH`; without it, OpenCode stays inventory-only. 4. **Cost** - character weight (`ceil(chars / 3.7)`) + init parser tool declarations. Model pricing auto-resolves by model name. 5. **Verdict** - REAP / KEEP / REVIEW with machine-readable reason. 6. **Act** - `reap prune` quarantines. `reap restore --all` undoes.
### Limitations (transparency) **Token counts are approximate.** The tool estimates tokens as `ceil(chars / 3.7)`, based on the average English BPE tokenizer rate. Real token counts vary by tokenizer (Claude vs GPT vs Gemini) and content (more code ≈ more tokens per char). This is a documented approximation - the relative ranking matters more than the absolute number. **Platform format stability.** Each supported platform has its own config layout and transcript format. These change over time as platforms evolve. Parser updates are an ongoing maintenance reality. The project is architected for easy fixes (one struct per platform in `internal/platform/`), but format changes can lag by days to weeks after a platform update. **OpenCode evidence needs the `sqlite3` CLI.** OpenCode stores session history in a SQLite database. skillreaper reads it through the system `sqlite3` binary in read-only mode - the real engine, so WAL-mode databases and overflow pages are handled correctly (a hand-rolled parser would not). No Go dependency is added. When `sqlite3` is **not** on `PATH`, OpenCode items have no usage evidence: they stay **REVIEW (never REAP)** with a warning at scan time. So do the skills in `~/.claude/skills`, which OpenCode loads too: one of them may be in use there, unseen. A history read only in part (a database too large for one query) counts as not read. The same safety net applies to any platform with no readable session transcripts. **Incomplete evidence never flags an item.** The scanner caps how much it reads per transcript record. If a record is oversized or unreadable, that platform's evidence is marked incomplete and its items stay **REVIEW (never REAP/MUTE)**, with a warning naming the platform - partial evidence can never mistakenly mark a tool as dead. The same holds for what reap cannot read elsewhere: a project folder that is a link to a disk that is not there, its own record of past uses, a CLAUDE.md, a `settings.json` or an agent's file. Each is named in a warning, and unused items stay REVIEW until it can be read. **An item that is new here waits out the grace period.** A skill or agent of your own is dated by its file; a server in a config, which has no date, by the day reap first found it. An item restored from quarantine or unmuted counts from that day too: it had no use while it was away. For `--grace-days` (14) after that it is REVIEW, and a bare `reap prune` leaves it. For an item that has existed for only part of the window, `--min-sessions` is scaled to that part. **A name in your CLAUDE.md protects a skill, a plain word only where it is written as a name.** A skill named in your CLAUDE.md or rules is kept (`claude-md-ref`). A name with a dash, a colon, an underscore or a digit in it (`code-review`, `ecc:plan`) counts wherever it stands. A one-word name (`review`) is also a word of the language, so it counts only where it is written as a name: `/review`, between backticks, asterisks or quotes, as a link's text, beside the word "skill", in a list item or a quoted line that begins with names (`- review: …`, `- review, deploy`, `> review`) or a heading of its own, or alone in a table cell. "always review the diff" protects nothing, and `reap why review` then says so. **A built-in command can count as a skill's use.** A transcript records `/plan` the same way whether it ran Claude Code's own command or a skill of yours named `plan`. reap counts it as a use of the skill, so such a skill is kept: when it cannot tell, it errs towards keeping. **One folder under two paths has two records.** What reap remembers about a config folder (uses seen before their transcripts were deleted, snapshots) is kept under the path you gave it. The same folder reached by two paths, through a link or as `/tmp/x` and `/private/tmp/x` on macOS, has two records: a run under one path does not see what a run under the other remembered, and `reap diff` does not find its snapshots. With the default `~/.claude` this never happens; with `--claude-dir`, write the folder one way. **Not a tool declaration fix.** Claude Code's deferred tools reduce the *init-time tool declaration* overhead. Skillreaper addresses a different problem: **always-loaded skill and agent descriptions.** If a skill description is 248 characters, it is read into context every session - regardless of lazy tool loading. These two optimizations are complementary, not competing.
### Design and internals - **100 % local**, zero dependencies, single static binary (Go ≥ 1.24) - **Multi-platform** - adding a new platform is one struct in `internal/platform/` - **Reversible quarantine** - prune moves, never deletes; the only permanent removal is `reap delete`, which you name and confirm - **MIT licensed** ``` cmd/reap/ CLI entry point internal/ platform/ platform definitions + auto-detection scan/ inventory scanners (claudemd.go: CLAUDE.md protection) usage/ transcript parser — tool_use + error tracking report/ verdict logic (REAP/MUTE/KEEP/REVIEW) + ANSI/JSON/MD renderers prune/ reversible quarantine mute/ description strip + backup/restore safepath/ shared path-confinement boundary (prune/mute/scan) atomicfile/ crash-safe writes (temp file + rename) hook/ SessionStart install/uninstall + nudge state cost/ model pricing readme/ maintainer-only README figure generator (not shipped) docs/ demo assets ```
--- ### Roadmap Tracked as issues, grouped by the problem they solve. - **The menu, next** - `reap reinvest` as its last step: what you removed becomes credit for a skill that covers work none of yours does, written from your own sessions (a command of its own today, and experimental); and the menu on Windows. - **Better verdicts** - `--since` / `--until` and a window that respects the corpus ([#53](https://github.com/thousandflowers/skillreaper/issues/53)); measuring wrong-tool picks ([#55](https://github.com/thousandflowers/skillreaper/issues/55)); two counters for a use, the ones you made and the automatic ones (a subagent's, or a line Claude Code adds by itself), so that a skill kept only by the second kind shows as such. Today both count as one. One record for a config folder reached by two paths (a link, `/tmp` and `/private/tmp`), with what both had remembered brought together. - **Act on more than one stack shape** - group skills by domain and language, then act on a group ([#101](https://github.com/thousandflowers/skillreaper/issues/101)); move a skill between user and workspace scope ([#102](https://github.com/thousandflowers/skillreaper/issues/102)). - **Teams** - shared policy with verdicts that stay on each machine ([#89](https://github.com/thousandflowers/skillreaper/issues/89)), and a hosted view of them ([#90](https://github.com/thousandflowers/skillreaper/issues/90)). Not planned: a CI job running `reap` (a runner has no session transcripts, so it would measure nothing - the periodic loop is `reap install-hook`), an extrapolated annual dollar figure, and git commit ranges (transcripts carry timestamps, so a window of days, `--days` today and `--since` / `--until` once #53 lands, covers it).
--- ### Where it is used Included in [awesome-go](https://github.com/avelino/awesome-go#artificial-intelligence) (182k ★, Artificial Intelligence section) and [awesome-agent-skills](https://github.com/VoltAgent/awesome-agent-skills#community-skills) (30k ★). Four external contributors, 19 merged commits. The verdict logic has been ported into another project with attribution in the code ([lean-agency](https://github.com/badithya-ms/lean-agency)).
--- ### Acknowledgements v0.2.0 ideas were inspired by work from the r/claudeskills community: - **[groundskeeper](https://github.com/zvoque/groundskeeper)** - SessionStart weekly nudge pattern and live usage tracking approach - **[optimize](https://github.com/codeprakhar25/optimize)** - name-only middle state (implemented as MUTE) and CLAUDE.md reference protection - Broken-vs-cold distinction direction inspired by discussion on r/claudeskills

<sub>Measured 2026-08-23 on my own installation; raw output in

<a href="docs/measurements/">docs/measurements/</a>. Every "on my own installation"

figure on this page comes from that one run.</sub>

One command. Zero config. It reads your real session transcripts, finds

every skill / MCP / agent your AI loads but never fires, and shows you exactly

what it costs you.

In a terminal, skillreaper opens [the menu](#the-menu): the same findings on

one screen, where you choose what goes and see the number fall before anything

is touched. reap prints the report, for reading, piping and agents.

<br>

What it does

skillreaper is a measuring instrument for your agent's context window.

Pruning is one of the things you do with the measurement, not the point of it.

The whole surface, in the order you use it:

| Stage | Command | What it answers |

|---|---|---|

| Measure | reap | What do I load, what actually fires, what does the dead part cost per session? |

| | reap gap | What share of each category is ever used, and which MCP tools fire but return noise? |

| | reap by-project | Which project is actually firing each skill? |

| Decide | reap why <name> | Why did *this* item get *this* verdict, on what evidence? |

| Act | reap prune | Quarantine the dead items, reversibly |

| | reap mute <name> | Strip a heavy rarely-used description, keep the skill callable |

| Engineer | reap route | Propose a lazy-load routing plan for a library too big to prune flat |

| | reap apm | Emit a proposed APM apm.yml, so a team reproduces one lean set |

| Compare | reap snapshot | Keep this run, so a later one has something to be measured against |

| | reap diff | What appeared, left, changed verdict, and did anything come back after a prune |

Everything above the Act row is read-only. You can run the entire

measurement side without changing a single file.

<br>

What it reads, what it writes

| Read-only, changes nothing | Writes, always reversible |

|---|---|

| reap <sup>1</sup> | reap prune  ↔  reap restore --all |

| reap gap <sup>1</sup> | reap mute <name>  ↔  reap unmute <name> |

| reap by-project <sup>1</sup> | reap keep <name>  ↔  reap keep --remove <name> |

| reap why <name> <sup>1</sup> | reap install-hook  ↔  reap uninstall-hook |

| reap route <sup>1</sup> | skillreaper / reap menu: the same writes, chosen on one screen, undone from it with u |

| reap apm <sup>1</sup> | |

| reap manifest <name> <sup>1</sup> | |

| reap share <sup>1</sup> | |

| reap snapshot <sup>1</sup> | |

| reap diff | |

Nothing is deleted unless you ask for exactly that. reap prune moves files

into a reaped/ directory with a versioned manifest, reap mute keeps a backup

of the description it strips, and reap uninstall-hook removes only

skillreaper's own entry, leaving your other hooks alone. The one exception is

the one you have to name: reap delete <name>, or d in the menu, removes an

item for good, says so in red, and asks first. Every edit of an existing file is

atomic (temp file + rename), so an interrupted prune, mute, or hook edit

leaves the original file intact, never a half-written mix, and every write stays

inside your home folder, in the files of the tools it reads (~/.claude,

~/.claude.json, ~/.codex and the like). Removing an MCP server edits

~/.claude.json and keeps a copy of the whole file in ~/.claude/reaped/backups/

until you restore that server; if Claude Code changes the file while reap is

editing it, reap writes nothing and asks you to run the command again.

One command is not local, and it is not in the table: reap reinvest, which is

experimental. It asks Claude, through claude -p, to read your sessions and

write a skill for work none of yours covers, and with --online it searches

skills.sh. Nothing else here calls a model or the network. (The menu's plugin

switch runs claude plugin disable, Claude Code's own command for that.)

<sub><sup>1</sup> The only files a read-only command writes are skillreaper's

own: <code>~/.claude/reaped/nudge-state.json</code>, which the default report

touches so a hint it already showed you does not repeat; a parsed-transcript

cache in your user cache folder, which keeps the next run fast; an evidence

record in your user config folder, which remembers uses older than your

transcripts; and the snapshot <code>reap snapshot</code> exists to write. None of

them touches your stack. <code>--no-nudge</code> (or

<code>SKILLREAPER_NO_NUDGE=1</code>) turns off the first and

<code>--no-cache</code> the second. No command in either column sends anything

over the network.</sub>

<br>

First 60 seconds

Three commands, in this order: measure, decide, act. Only the third one

writes anything, and it prints its own undo line.


reap

reap why import-timesheet

reap prune

import-timesheet stands for any name in your own report.

Or all three on one screen: skillreaper, [the menu](#the-menu).

With npx and nothing installed there is no reap on your PATH: write

npx skillreaper where these lines say reap (npx skillreaper why <name>).

1. reap prints the report: the same rows as the block at the top of this

page (that one is reap --agent), grouped by verdict, with the reason in each

group's title and in a NOTE column. Every row carries a verdict:

| Label | Meaning |

|---|---|

| REAP(broken) | Invoked but errored - broken, not just cold |

| REAP | Zero uses - safe to quarantine |

| MUTE | Used rarely + heavy - description stripped, skill stays available |

| KEEP | Used, tiny, manually protected, or at work with no use of its own |

| REVIEW | Too new, not enough sessions, or used in a way reap cannot weigh |

| - | Not judged: something you muted, a hook, a prose file, an MCP server seen only in your transcripts |

Every verdict includes a reason suffix explaining *why*, and an item whose

evidence was incomplete stays REVIEW rather than being flagged. The reasons:

| Reason | With | It means |

|---|---|---|

| unused | REAP | never fired, with enough sessions to judge |

| broken | REAP | invoked, and it only ever errored |

| heavy-rare | MUTE | used, but heavy and in too few sessions |

| used | KEEP | used in this window |

| tiny | KEEP | weighs almost nothing |

| keep | KEEP | you protected it with reap keep |

| claude-md-ref | KEEP | named in your CLAUDE.md or rules |

| hook-loaded | KEEP | a SessionStart hook reads it into the session |

| agent-loaded | KEEP | an agent names it under skills: and loads it when it starts |

| main-agent | KEEP | your settings run the session as this agent |

| skill-agent | KEEP | a skill names it under agent: and runs in it |

| grace | REVIEW | new here: installed, added, restored or unmuted too recently to judge |

| needs-data | REVIEW | not enough sessions yet |

| rare | REVIEW | fired before this window, on a longer cadence |

| no-transcript | REVIEW | evidence about it is missing: this tool's sessions, or a file that could protect it, cannot be read |

| used-elsewhere | REVIEW | another tool that loads the same folder used it |

| muted | - | you muted it, so its uses prove nothing |

2. reap why <name> is how you argue with a verdict before acting on it.

It shows the whole case for one item, so you are not trusting a label:

3. reap prune asks before it moves anything, quarantines what you confirm

into reaped/, and ends by printing reap restore --all. If a verdict looks

wrong, reap keep <name> protects the item permanently instead.

<p align="center"><sub>The <code>why</code> output above is real, produced

against the same generated sample stack as the report at the top of this page

(<a href="docs/gif-helpers/hero-fixture.sh">hero-fixture.sh</a>) - so the item

names are the fixture's, not anyone's install.</sub></p>

<br>

Why this exists

Why I built this

I was running out of context budget on every session. I had accumulated skills,

MCP servers, and agents over months most of them experiments I'd forgotten

about or be too busy to change it. Every new session loaded all of them, burning tokens before I'd typed a

single message.

I needed to know which ones were actually firing and which were just dead

weight. Nothing existing told me that from transcript evidence. So I built it.

It now supports every platform in the table below, and ships on Homebrew, npm,

and as a static binary for every major OS.

<br>

Two costs of context bloat

Wrong-tool picks. Buried in a wall of irrelevant options, your agent

wastes turns reaching for the wrong tool. More turns = slower, costlier,

sloppier runs. This isn't about pennies - it's about work quality.

Wasted tokens. Dead instructions eat context every session and hurt

prompt-cache hit rate. A typical setup:

<!-- readme-mine-costs:start -->

  • 382 items loaded
  • 369 never fired (96 %), of which 367 marked REAP
  • 19 755 tok/session dead
  • ~1 087 000 tok/month burned on irrelevant instructions
  • ~$3.26/month, ~$39/year - the same waste priced instead of counted

<p align="center"><sub>The money line is one measurement of one stack, n=1, and the

weakest number here: <code>19 755 × 55 × $3.00 ÷ 1e6</code> - input tokens only, at

<code>claude-sonnet-4-6</code>'s $3.00/MTok default, with tokens estimated as

<code>ceil(chars / 3.7)</code> and the monthly session count extrapolated from a

30-day window. Change the model, the price, or how much you work and it moves;

the item and token counts do not. See <a href="#limitations-transparency">Limitations</a>.</sub></p>

<p align="center"><em>Measured on my own setup - 55 sessions over 30 days, 2026-08-23. Run <code>reap</code> to see yours.</em></p>

<!-- readme-mine-costs:end -->

skillreaper measures both, from evidence - no guessing.

> reap points at the waste. You decide what goes.

<br>

Privacy

100 % local, with one exception you start by hand. Zero telemetry, zero

uploads. Reads config files and session transcripts on disk, and your data never

leaves your machine, except through reap reinvest: it is experimental, says so

on its first line, and sends Claude, through claude -p on your own Claude Code

account, excerpts of your sessions (with the keys it recognises removed first)

and the names and descriptions of your installed skills. With --online it also

sends search words drawn from them to skills.sh (and, with --mcp, the MCP

registry, then asks npm, PyPI and GitHub about the servers it finds), and says

that too on its first line. It keeps what it read of your sessions, with the

keys removed, in sessions_memory.json under reap's state folder

(~/Library/Application Support/skillreaper/reinvest on macOS), readable by

you alone, so that a kind of work is still known after Claude Code deletes

the transcripts.

<br>

Before → After: what removing token waste buys

<!-- readme-mine-table:start -->

| Before skillreaper | After skillreaper |

|---|---|

| 382 items loaded every session | 15 kept · 13 actually fire |

| 19 755 tok/session dead | Full context budget for real work |

| ≈ 73 000 dead chars ≈ 29 pages every session (at 500 words/pg) | Zero |

| Lower cache hit rate = higher latency | Smaller prompt fits in cache |

Getting started

Install

Inside Claude Code - adds /skillreaper:reap and /skillreaper:gap, so the

report renders in the conversation instead of a scrollback you have to re-read:


/plugin marketplace add thousandflowers/skillreaper

/plugin install skillreaper@skillreaper

The plugin is a thin wrapper: it drives the same binary, so install that too

with any line below. If the skills can't find it, they print how to run it with

npx skillreaper and how to install it permanently.

Install permanently - Homebrew and npm install both names, reap and

skillreaper, so either one works. go install gives you reap:

Pick one. macOS, with Homebrew:


brew install thousandflowers/tap/skillreaper

Any platform, with npm (downloads the matching prebuilt, checksum-verified):


npm install -g skillreaper

Any platform, with Go 1.24 or newer:


go install github.com/thousandflowers/skillreaper/cmd/reap@latest

> Already installed it with Homebrew? You don't need the npm package -

> both put reap and skillreaper in the same prefix, so npm install -g

> stops at an EEXIST link error rather than overwriting brew's copy.

> Pick one route: to switch to npm, run brew uninstall skillreaper first.

> Neither affects npx skillreaper, which runs from a cache and never

> links a global command.

Binary downloads - macOS (Intel + Apple Silicon), Linux (amd64 + arm64),

Windows (amd64 + arm64) - all on the

releases page.

Single static binary, no dependencies.

Upgrading, uninstalling, and platform-specific tips →

[INSTALL.md](INSTALL.md).

The menu


skillreaper

reap menu opens the same screen.

<p align="center">

<img src="docs/menu-demo.gif" alt="The skillreaper menu: choosing what to prune and mute, the number falling to zero, then the receipt" width="900"><br>

<sub>Recorded against an invented stack

One screen instead of three commands. The number at the top is what you re-send

| space | Takes reap's own suggestion for the row, the group or the selection |

| p m l d | Prune, mute, lock, delete. Delete is the one choice that cannot be undone, and it says so in red |

| n   u | Clear a choice  ·  undo a mute, a lock or a prune that is already on disk |

| a | Fills in what reap suggests; pressed again, puts back what was there. Where reap is not sure it fills in nothing: those rows are yours to choose, one by one |

| o | Turns the row's whole plugin off, through claude plugin disable |

| enter | Opens a group, or a row's card: its weight, its last use, why reap says what it says |

| shift+↑↓   v   mouse | Select many rows at once; a click takes reap's suggestion, a drag paints it |

| tab | Money or tokens. On a subscription it starts with tokens: they are what eats the plan |

| g   f | Group by suggestion, by plugin, or flat  ·  one platform at a time |

| hold s | Shows what reap suggests on every row, while you hold it |

| shift+enter | The receipt, then y applies. Where Shift cannot be read (ssh, some Linux terminals) the key is x, and the footer says so |

Any action can be chosen on any row or group. reap's verdicts are suggestions

and never limit the choice; it refuses only what is physically impossible, and

says why on the row.

What the menu does that the commands do not, all on macOS and all local:

  • Amounts are shown in the currency set on your Mac (or the locale in LC_ALL

or LC_MONETARY, when you set one), at a fixed ECB reference rate shipped

inside the release. Nothing is fetched. A release whose table is

more than 90 days old shows US dollars instead of a stale conversion.

  • Terminal.app sends Shift+arrows and Shift+Enter as the plain keys, so while

the menu is open a small /usr/bin/osascript helper asks macOS whether Shift

(and the s key, for the peek) is down. It reads those two keys' state and

nothing else, needs no permission, writes nothing, and exits with the menu. It

does not run over ssh.

The menu runs on macOS and Linux. On Windows, in a pipe, or with any argument,

skillreaper prints the report as it always did, and reap alone always does.

Beyond pruning

route - context engineering for large tool libraries

After pruning, a library of hundreds of legit skills still grows resident

context linearly. reap route proposes a category-router organization driven by

real firing evidence, not text similarity: frequently-fired skills stay

exposed; the rare long tail is pushed behind leaf routers (grouped by namespace,

else dominant firing project) loaded on demand. It is strictly opt-in and

secondary to pruning - and below ~150 skills, native loading is usually enough,

so the plan says so. The output is a plan: proposed, never auto-applied.

| reap route --json | JSON |

| reap route --route-min-skills 200 | Only show a plan past 200 surviving skills |

snapshot and diff - what changed since last time

A report is a photograph. The questions that recur are comparative: did a

pruned item come back, is the bloat growing or shrinking after a prune.

reap snapshot writes the run's --json payload beside the evidence digest.

reap diff compares two of them, newest against previous by default, and

reports what appeared, what left, what changed verdict, and the movement in

dead tokens and utilization.

The case it exists to catch leads the output: **an item that is back after

being pruned**. Plugin and marketplace updates reinstall silently, and that

line is read from the prune manifest rather than guessed from the two

snapshots, so it says "this tool removed it and it returned" rather than

"something is different". An item you restored yourself is not reported, since

that was deliberate.

|---|---|

| reap snapshot | Save this run |

| reap diff | Newest vs previous |

| reap diff <a> <b> | Two named snapshots |

| reap diff --json | Structured output |

Snapshots are never taken automatically: state nobody asked for is the disease

this tool treats. Take one with reap snapshot when you want a point to compare

against. The hook reap install-hook installs only nudges; a periodic snapshot

would belong there, and is not there yet.

Transparency and internals

Platform support

| Platform | Full support |

|---|---|

| Claude Code | ✅ |

| Codex CLI | ✅ for what was used (its history shows what fired, not everything that was used, so an item with no use there surfaces as REVIEW, never REAP or MUTE) |

| Hermes | Inventory only (session history is in state.db, which skillreaper does not parse yet, so its items surface as REVIEW, never REAP) |

| OpenCode | ✅ (usage evidence needs the sqlite3 CLI; inventory-only without it) |

| Cursor | Inventory only (no local transcripts) |

| OpenClaw | Inventory only (no session history) |

| Gemini CLI | Inventory only (session history is stored in a layout skillreaper does not parse yet, so its items surface as REVIEW, never REAP) |

<br>

How the evidence is gathered

1. Auto-detect - probes every known config directory. Only installed

platforms are scanned. No flags needed.

2. Inventory - scans skills, agents, MCP servers, hooks, and prose

files across all detected platforms.

3. Evidence - parses JSONL session transcripts (Claude Code, Codex CLI).

Counts tool_use blocks and command invocations with timestamps.

OpenCode's SQLite history is read via the sqlite3 CLI (read-only) when it

is on PATH; without it, OpenCode stays inventory-only.

4. Cost - character weight (ceil(chars / 3.7)) + init parser tool

declarations. Model pricing auto-resolves by model name.

5. Verdict - REAP / KEEP / REVIEW with machine-readable reason.

6. Act - reap prune quarantines. reap restore --all undoes.

<br>

Limitations (transparency)

Token counts are approximate. The tool estimates tokens as

ceil(chars / 3.7), based on the average English BPE tokenizer rate.

Real token counts vary by tokenizer (Claude vs GPT vs Gemini) and content

(more code ≈ more tokens per char). This is a documented approximation -

the relative ranking matters more than the absolute number.

Platform format stability. Each supported platform has its own config

layout and transcript format. These change over time as platforms evolve.

Parser updates are an ongoing maintenance reality. The project is architected

for easy fixes (one struct per platform in internal/platform/), but format

changes can lag by days to weeks after a platform update.

OpenCode evidence needs the sqlite3 CLI. OpenCode stores session history

in a SQLite database. skillreaper reads it through the system sqlite3 binary

in read-only mode - the real engine, so WAL-mode databases and overflow pages

are handled correctly (a hand-rolled parser would not). No Go dependency is

added. When sqlite3 is not on PATH, OpenCode items have no usage

evidence: they stay REVIEW (never REAP) with a warning at scan time. So do

the skills in ~/.claude/skills, which OpenCode loads too: one of them may be

in use there, unseen. A history read only in part (a database too large for

one query) counts as not read. The same safety net applies to any platform

with no readable session transcripts.

Incomplete evidence never flags an item. The scanner caps how much it

reads per transcript record. If a record is oversized or unreadable, that

platform's evidence is marked incomplete and its items stay **REVIEW (never

REAP/MUTE)**, with a warning naming the platform - partial evidence can never

mistakenly mark a tool as dead. The same holds for what reap cannot read

elsewhere: a project folder that is a link to a disk that is not there, its

own record of past uses, a CLAUDE.md, a settings.json or an agent's file.

Each is named in a warning, and unused items stay REVIEW until it can be read.

An item that is new here waits out the grace period. A skill or agent of

your own is dated by its file; a server in a config, which has no date, by the

day reap first found it. An item restored from quarantine or unmuted counts

from that day too: it had no use while it was away. For --grace-days (14)

after that it is REVIEW, and a bare reap prune leaves it. For an item that

has existed for only part of the window, --min-sessions is scaled to that

part.

**A name in your CLAUDE.md protects a skill, a plain word only where it is

written as a name.** A skill named in your CLAUDE.md or rules is kept

(claude-md-ref). A name with a dash, a colon, an underscore or a digit in

it (code-review, ecc:plan) counts wherever it stands. A one-word name

(review) is also a word of the language, so it counts only where it is

written as a name: /review, between backticks, asterisks or quotes, as a

link's text, beside the word "skill", in a list item or a quoted line that

begins with names (- review: …, - review, deploy, > review) or a heading

of its own, or alone in a table cell. "always review the diff" protects nothing, and reap why review

then says so.

A built-in command can count as a skill's use. A transcript records

/plan the same way whether it ran Claude Code's own command or a skill of

yours named plan. reap counts it as a use of the skill, so such a skill is

kept: when it cannot tell, it errs towards keeping.

One folder under two paths has two records. What reap remembers about a

config folder (uses seen before their transcripts were deleted, snapshots) is

kept under the path you gave it. The same folder reached by two paths, through

a link or as /tmp/x and /private/tmp/x on macOS, has two records: a run

under one path does not see what a run under the other remembered, and `reap

diff does not find its snapshots. With the default ~/.claude` this never

happens; with --claude-dir, write the folder one way.

Not a tool declaration fix. Claude Code's deferred tools reduce the

*init-time tool declaration* overhead. Skillreaper addresses a different

problem: always-loaded skill and agent descriptions. If a skill description

is 248 characters, it is read into context every session - regardless of

lazy tool loading. These two optimizations are complementary, not competing.

  • 100 % local, zero dependencies, single static binary (Go ≥ 1.24)
  • Multi-platform - adding a new platform is one struct in

  • Reversible quarantine - prune moves, never deletes; the only permanent removal is reap delete, which you name and confirm
  • MIT licensed

internal/

  platform/     platform definitions + auto-detection

  scan/         inventory scanners (claudemd.go: CLAUDE.md protection)

  usage/        transcript parser — tool_use + error tracking

  report/       verdict logic (REAP/MUTE/KEEP/REVIEW) + ANSI/JSON/MD renderers

  prune/        reversible quarantine

  mute/         description strip + backup/restore

  safepath/     shared path-confinement boundary (prune/mute/scan)
